lines.text: A courthouse built on a gallows. A battlefield that still gives directions. A cemetery stormed by vampire hunters. Five real places, partner, where people swear the dead never left. Let's go see them.
San Diego, 1852. A man called Yankee Jim Robinson was hanged on this spot, for stealing a boat.
A man named Thomas Whaley watched the hanging. A few years later, he bought the land.
In 1857 he finished the city's first two story brick house... right on the gallows site.
It became a store, a theater, even the county courthouse.
And the family heard heavy footsteps upstairs, when no one was there. They decided it was Yankee Jim.
Today it's a museum. And visitors still report footsteps.
Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. July 1863. In just three days, more than fifty thousand men were killed, wounded, captured or lost.
On July second, Confederate troops fought their way into a maze of giant boulders called Devil's Den.
Today it's a national park. And the rangers tell a story about it.
A visitor said a ragged man in a floppy hat, barefoot, walked up to her and said: what you're looking for is over there. Then he was gone.
The rangers said she'd just described exactly what a Texas soldier looked like in 1863.
London. Highgate Cemetery. A grand Victorian graveyard that, by the late nineteen sixties, was overgrown and crumbling.
Then the stories started. A tall grey figure, seen drifting between the tombs.
Two rival occult investigators went on television. One said it wasn't a ghost at all. It was a vampire. And he announced a hunt.
Friday the thirteenth of March, 1970. By nightfall, crowds were climbing the walls with stakes and crosses. Police couldn't hold them back.
No vampire was ever found. But the legend never left. Today Highgate is restored, and open for tours.
The Tower of London. A fortress on the River Thames for nearly a thousand years. A palace, a prison... and a place of execution.
In 1536, Queen Anne Boleyn was beheaded inside these walls. She's buried in the Tower's own chapel.
October 1817. The Keeper of the Crown Jewels, Edmund Swifte, sat down to supper with his family in the Jewel House.
He later wrote that a glowing tube, like bubbling blue liquid, appeared above the table... and moved toward his wife.

1864. A soldier was found collapsed at his post. Charged with sleeping on duty, he said a white figure came at him... and his bayonet went straight through it. Other soldiers backed up his story. He was cleared.
Philadelphia. Eastern State Penitentiary. It opened in 1829, built like a castle, with cell blocks spreading out like the spokes of a wheel.
The idea was total solitude. Prisoners lived alone, ate alone, and worked alone... for years.
In 1929, Al Capone arrived. He spent eight months here. His cell had rugs, lamps, and a radio. But he didn't sleep well.
Legend says guards could hear him at night, begging someone to leave him alone. Capone believed it was a man killed in the Saint Valentine's Day Massacre.
The prison closed in 1971. And in Cellblock 12, staff and visitors report voices and laughter, echoing down an empty hall.
Five places. Five stories the dead just won't let go of. Which one would you spend a night in, alone? Tell me in the comments. Subscribe for more files. I'll be waiting, partner.
